title: Deciding the Attainability of the Multiparameter Quantum Fisher Information is NP-Hard
authors: Lorcan O. Conlon, Laura Shou, V Vijendran, Kishor Bharti, Aritra Das, Simon K. Yung, Jacob M. Taylor, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Jun Suzuki, Syed M. Assad
abstract: The quantum Fisher information (QFI) sets a fundamental bound on the attainable precision when estimating multiple parameters simultaneously. Incompatibility among the individually optimal measurements can, in some cases, imply that the precision limit set by the QFI is not attainable. In certain special cases, including pure states and full-rank states, the exact conditions for when the precision limit set by the QFI can be saturated are known. However, general conditions for the attainability of the QFI with measurements on individual copies of the quantum state have long been sought. Indeed, this was recently stated as one of the five problems in quantum information theory highlighted by [P. Horodecki et al, PRX Quantum 3, 010101 (2022)]. In this work we prove that exact attainability with individual measurements is NP-hard to decide, even for a restricted set of real, constant-rank quantum models. The source problem for our proof is the NP-hard problem of deciding whether a given bipartite density matrix is separable or not. Our result shows that the longstanding difficulty in obtaining general conditions for QFI attainability reflects a fundamental computational obstruction, rather than merely a limitation of existing mathematical techniques: unless P=NP, no efficiently computable necessary-and-sufficient criterion can exist in general.
summary: This paper proves that determining if the theoretical precision limit set by the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) is actually achievable in quantum parameter estimation is an NP-hard problem. By reducing the problem to the known hard problem of matrix separability, the authors show that a general, efficient criterion for QFI attainability cannot exist unless P=NP.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental question of determining whether the precision limit set by the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) for estimating multiple parameters is actually attainable using individual measurements on a quantum state.
main_result: They prove that deciding QFI attainability is NP-hard, establishing a fundamental computational barrier: unless P=NP, no efficient general criterion for attainability can exist.
method: The proof relies on a polynomial-time reduction from the known NP-hard problem of determining the separability of a bipartite density matrix to the QFI attainability decision problem.
model_or_system: The analysis concerns quantum parameter estimation in a general quantum state $\rho(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_p)$ within a $D$-dimensional Hilbert space, utilizing the framework of Symmetric Logarithmic Derivatives (SLDs).
key_observables: The Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix ($J_Q$) and the covariance matrix ($V$) derived from the measurement POVM are the key observables used to test the attainability condition $V = J_Q^{-1}$.
important_parameters: The number of parameters ($p$), the dimension of the Hilbert space ($D$), and the structure of the quantum model are important parameters.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the computational complexity class P $\neq$ NP, which underpins the hardness result. The analysis also considers restricted models like real, constant-rank quantum models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically maps the NP-hard problem of matrix separability to the problem of QCRB attainability, illustrating the reduction used in the proof.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the QFI bound, frames the attainability as a decision problem, and then constructs a specific quantum encoding model that maps the hard separability problem instance to the QFI attainability question, proving the NP-hardness.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep theoretical constraint on quantum metrology, showing that even calculating the best possible precision bound (QFI) does not guarantee that the bound is physically achievable without solving an NP-hard problem.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic depiction of main results. The left and right outer blue ovals denote the set of all matri- ces Y of a certain dimension and the corresponding set of multiparameter estimation problems defined in Theorem 3 respectively. In this work, we map the problem of deciding whether a given matrix Y is separable or not to the problem of deciding whether the QCRB is attainable (Theorem 3). As it is known that deciding whether a bipartite density matrix is separable or not is NP-hard (Theorem 2), this im- plies that deciding whether the QCRB is attainable or not is also NP-hard (Theorem 4).
